author: Jeremy Allen
review_text:
Dutch producer Jochem Paap's first album in two decades is a proud ripose to the vicissitudes of the algorithm, finds Jeremy Allen

With more than 43 million songs uploaded to streaming services every year, how does one avert overload fatigue from the sheer mass of new music? It's a modern reality that the Dutch music producer Jochem Paap has been wrestling with, with Walkman his first solo release in twenty years. The name of this record harks back to the Sony Walkman, of course, the mobile cassette player that revolutionised personal listening in the 1980s and set us on our way towards the iPod and streaming platforms listened to via smartphones.

If that gives an impression that Walkman might be a retreat into a halcyon past where analogue technology ruled supreme, then, thankfully, you'd be mistaken. Speedy J's long-awaited new album is made up of one hour and thirty minutes of music, specifically long enough to fit onto two sides of a C90 cassette, and ideal for an extended ramble across areas of outstanding natural beauty or the hubbub of the city – with or without a dog. Nevertheless, the music therein is anything but backward-looking, embracing electronic experimentation and throwing up a variety of textures and moods to influence and alter the experience of travelling on foot or whatever else you might be up to.

Opener 'Arp Δmp Chasm' brings immediate urgency, buzzing with a fluctuating noise that mimics the function of organ stoppers, channelled through distorted frequencies to amp up tension. That tension is then lipped into 'Drift Vector', which inhabits a subterranean intersection where techno, drum'n'bass and dub all align. 'ModLoop 138/Fragment' then brings a flurry of overdriven digital music that could have been written on a circuit board, and probably was.

There are a number of shorter tracks here that feel as though they could be developed further, such as the wobbly, translucent 'Nachtgrain'. But if that number might have threatened to become soporific, the glitchy, nagging, invasive 'Chronoroute Fank' immediately smacks the listener out of any impassivity. Longest by some distance is the near 15-minute exploration in sound that is 'JT33Unstable Core', the penultimate track, which seems to traverse a plain of corrugated iron like a xenomorph in 60mph winds – at least until peels of feedback break through and transcend into a pleasant higher place, reminiscent of Stars of the Lid at their most beatific.

These tracks certainly work in isolation, though arranged as they are by Paap as curator, they create their own narrative that the listener then provides the visuals for. That probably seems obvious – and it is – though these tacit suggestions on how to consume are at least a way of reclaiming some agency where music is concerned, after it was so comprehensively hijacked and subjugated by big tech.
